issues.legal_issue: The compensation framework for acquiring property that was previously requisitioned does not violate equality merely because it omits separate awards of solatium and interest available under the general land acquisition law.
material_facts: The property had first been requisitioned, and compensation was payable for the owner’s loss of possession and enjoyment during requisition.

The later acquisition concerned the remaining ownership rights, and the governing framework valued the property by the price it would have fetched in the open market on the acquisition date, assuming it remained in its condition at requisition.
The acquiring authority was required to determine just compensation with regard to the circumstances of the case and the statutory compensation principles.
The owners argued that the absence of separate solatium and interest, unlike under the Land Acquisition Act, amounted to discrimination.
issues.conclusion: The omission of separate solatium and interest under the compensation framework does not make it discriminatory or violative of Article 14. The compensation must be determined under the governing Act; the general land acquisition provisions cannot be imported merely because they provide those additional amounts.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require identical compensation regimes where the acquisitions differ materially. Under Sections 7(3) and 8(1), 8(2) and 8(3)(a) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, an arbitrator determines just compensation in light of the case’s circumstances and the prescribed open-market valuation. Requisition compensation accounts for the earlier loss of possession and enjoyment, so a subsequent acquisition is not equivalent to acquisition of the entire ownership interest under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Court distinguished Vajravelu Mudaliar, Balammal, Nagpur Improvement Trust and State of Kerala v. T.M. Peter, and relied on the reasoning in Union of India v. Kamlabhai Harjiwandas Parekh and Prakash Amichand Shah; it also distinguished P.C. Goswami because the Assam statute there permitted application of the Land Acquisition Act. Sections 23 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act do not apply simply by comparison, and solatium is not mandatory in every acquisition.

rule.if: acquisition_after_prior_requisition and requisition_compensation_paid_for_possession_and_enjoyment and acquisition_covers_remaining_ownership_rights and compensation_uses_open_market_value and proceeding_challenges_compensation_equality

predicates.acquisition_after_prior_requisition: The property was requisitioned before it was acquired.
predicates.requisition_compensation_paid_for_posses: Compensation was payable for the owner’s loss of possession and enjoyment during requisition.
predicates.acquisition_covers_remaining_ownership_r: The later acquisition concerned ownership rights remaining after the earlier requisition.
predicates.compensation_uses_open_market_value: The compensation framework values the property by its open-market price at acquisition, assessed on the prescribed basis.
predicates.proceeding_challenges_compensation_equal: The proceeding challenges the compensation framework as unequal because it differs from another acquisition regime.

issues.definition: When property is acquired after requisition, the earlier requisition is compensated for, the later acquisition concerns the remaining ownership rights, and compensation is assessed on an open-market basis, a challenge based only on different compensation treatment does not establish unconstitutional discrimination.

issues.legal_issue: An enactment’s later inclusion in the protected schedule gives it retrospective protection against a fundamental-rights challenge, subject to the limitation that a post-cutoff constitutional amendment must not damage or destroy the Constitution’s basic structure.
material_facts: The challenged Act was added to the Ninth Schedule after the date identified in the Court’s discussion of the basic-structure limitation.
The challenge alleged that the compensation provision violated Article 14.
The Court had concluded that the compensation provision did not violate Article 14.
issues.conclusion: The inclusion protects the Act retrospectively from the Article 14 challenge in these appeals because the provision was not discriminatory. The Court therefore applied the rule in Jagannath; the challenge based on damage to the basic structure did not succeed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B gives retrospective protection to Acts included in the Ninth Schedule against challenges based on Part III rights, notwithstanding prior judicial decisions. Jagannath v. Authorised Officer, Land Reforms states that inclusion can cure such a defect retrospectively. Under Waman Rao v. Union of India, additions made after April 24, 1973 are protected only if the constitutional amendment making the addition does not damage or destroy the Constitution’s basic structure. Since the Court found no Article 14 violation, the basic-structure objection did not alter the result.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_scheduled_la: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law that is included in a protected constitutional schedule.
predicates.law_added_to_protected_schedule: The law was added to the protected schedule by a constitutional amendment.
predicates.alleged_rights_violation_not_established: The court finds that the alleged fundamental-rights violation has not been established.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges a law included in a protected schedule and the alleged fundamental-rights violation is not established, the law receives retrospective protection from that challenge.

issues.legal_issue: A substantial and unexplained delay in appointing an arbitrator can justify retaining exceptional compensation relief despite the ordinary compensation framework.
material_facts: In some appeals, no arbitrator had been appointed for sixteen years.
The awards in those cases granted solatium and interest.
The Court relied on its earlier decision granting such relief in view of a comparable delay and noted that the law had meanwhile been amended to provide solatium and interest.
issues.conclusion: The Court left the awards of solatium and interest undisturbed in those appeals and dismissed them, applying the principle in Harbans Singh Shanni Devi v. Union of India to the exceptional delay.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied its case-specific ruling in Harbans Singh Shanni Devi v. Union of India, which granted solatium and interest where the Union had failed to appoint an arbitrator for sixteen years, taking account of the intervening amendment to the law. The relief was justified by the peculiar circumstances and does not establish that solatium and interest are generally payable under the Act.

predicates.appeal_against_compensation_award: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an award of compensation.
predicates.arbitrator_appointment_severely_delayed: The responsible authority failed to appoint an arbitrator for a prolonged period.
predicates.award_grants_exceptional_compensation_re: The award granted additional compensation relief in response to the circumstances of the case.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning a compensation award, prolonged failure to appoint an arbitrator can support leaving exceptional additional compensation relief in place.

issues.legal_issue: A previously challenged original compensation award that has become final cannot be reopened, although a later enhancement found to be unlawful may be set aside.
material_facts: The original award had been challenged in an earlier petition for special leave, which was dismissed.
A later award enhanced the compensation.
The Court found the enhanced award impermissible, while treating the original award as final.
issues.conclusion: The original award remained final and could not be reopened; the Court set aside only the unlawful enhancement.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the dismissal of the earlier challenge as rendering the original award final and res judicata, while separately holding that the later enhancement was impermissible.

predicates.appeal_against_compensation_award: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a compensation award.
predicates.earlier_challenge_to_original_award_dism: An earlier challenge to the original award was dismissed.
predicates.later_enhancement_found_unlawful: The court finds that a subsequent enhancement of the award was unlawful.

issues.definition: When an earlier challenge to the original award was dismissed, that award remains final, but an unlawful later enhancement may be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation determination that has stood unchallenged for a very long time may be left undisturbed in view of the elapsed time and the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The award had been made in 1961.
The Court settled the legal question while considering the appeal more than three decades after the award.
The Court considered the elapsed time and the particular circumstances before deciding whether to interfere.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to disturb the award and dismissed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its discretion in light of the particular circumstances and the very long time that had elapsed since the award; it did not state a general rule that old awards are immune from review.

predicates.appeal_against_compensation_award: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a compensation award.
predicates.award_has_stood_without_interference: The award remained in place without being disturbed after it was made.
predicates.substantial_time_elapsed_since_award: A very long period elapsed between the award and the court’s consideration of the appeal.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning an award that has remained in place for a very long time, the court may leave it undisturbed in the particular circumstances.
